@NASAAdmin makes the case that walking on the Moon won't be reserved for government astronauts alone, we'll see commercial or private misions will be coming.

Let me just first say that having an aviation background is hardly a requirement anymore. If you think about what a crew of astronauts should look like, having one or two people with that background important and helpful for sure if you want I think number one in this and this also very much qualifies Peter is medical professionasl. The technology to enable humans to go to Mars is going to happen far faster or sooner than having the countermeasures in place for how demanding physiologically it is to be in space. I just don't ever see a a world in our lifetime where you're not going to have considerable investments in medical professionals supporting outposts on the moon and certainly Mars someday. There will always be a need for for NASA astronauts. And I'd be shocked if you didn't see at some point in time that NASA astronauts played a role in helping train and certify commercial or private crews going on those missions.

Cook adds helpful color about why supply constraints will be more significant in September. 

Cook says iPhone 22% and Mac 29% growth in June was much better than expected so they pulled supply forward into June from September "and will have one quarter that they will be scrambling for supply".

The $AAPL guide is not as bad as it first looks. Stock now down 8%, at after-hours lows. 

Bottom line: Doing the math, if not for FX and supply constraints, I believe the September revenue guide would have called for up 15% yy in September vs Street at up 12%.

Here's how I get there:

* For September the Street was at 12% growth.
They guided 9-11%.

* Cook says the supply constraints to increase significantly in September. The "significantly increase supply constraints" will hide what the underlying demand actually is.

* FX was a 2.5% q/q negative impact to growth. 

* Adding back the FX was 2.5% gets us to 11.5% and 13.5%. They typically come in at the high end.

tweets.text: There is nothing more important than understanding how reality works and how to deal with it. The state of mind you bring to this process makes all the difference. I have found it helpful to think of my life as if it were a game in which each problem I face is a puzzle I need to solve. By solving the puzzle, I get a gem in the form of a principle that helps me avoid the same sort of problem in the future. Collecting these gems continually improves my decision making, so I am able to ascend to higher and higher levels of play in which the game gets harder and the stakes become ever greater. #principleoftheday

tweets.text:
Crypto isn't about the shitty coin you bought.

That's the mistake many people make… lose money on a token, decide the whole thing is a scam, and walk away angry. All while the story keeps playing out around them.

Blockchain is the coordination layer for the digital economy.

It's how AI agents make payments at machine speed. It's how identity, privacy, and value move across the internet when humans aren't the primary users anymore.

AI and blockchain are married at the hip. Every agent, autonomous transaction, piece of the machine economy that's arriving now needs a programmable layer to run on. That's what the layer 1s actually are.

Own a piece of it, and you own a piece of the agent economy.

The sell pressure felt really extreme for trad markets, this kind of "no bounce allowed" price action is usually what we see in crypto but not in stocks, so it really makes sense that we have an explanation now... which is the "Leopold situation".

As I said in my tweet below, the core AI long positions remain unchanged but I definitely took some profits here on the short-term dip buying.
I was playing for a strong bounce, and it was a bit painful to wait for it (SNDK had wild swings around the $1000 bottom / MU had a 'delayed' leg down yesterday, etc), but here we finally have it, and we have it big time (+40% rebound)

tweets.text:
This is basically the first step of the hard takeoff scenario. So it’s not “AI suddenly wakes up and becomes a god”, but AI starts improving the system that runs and trains AI, in domains where progress is measurable and verifiable.

GPT-5.6 Sol is already analyzing production traffic, finding load-balancing inefficiencies, testing new routing strategies, rewriting GPU kernels and validating the results. Those kernel optimizations cut serving costs by 20% (so billions of $$$)

It also designed and ran hundreds of experiments to improve its own speculative decoding model, launched the training runs, monitored them, and intervened when hardware failed or training became unstable. Result: 15%+ more token-generation efficiency (which means freeing more compute and reducing cost). 

This is recursive self-improvement in its early, very practical form! The model improves the engineering stack, which makes the model cheaper and faster, which gives researchers more compute and more experiments, which produces a better model…

Today this works best in software engineering because the output is easy to measure: does the kernel compile, is it correct, is latency lower, did cost go down? Soon the same loop moves into AI research itself: experiment design, architecture search, training recipes, data generation, evals, debugging training runs.

At that point it is no longer just “AI helping engineers work faster.” It is AI accelerating the process that creates the next AI. 

That is the hard takeoff path to the singularity (AGI). Not one magical jump, but a feedback loop that keeps getting faster. If you want to be fancy you can say: « This is the beginning of a recursive self-improvement loop toward the singularity. »
